summary: Pupils aged 9–11 learn that many everyday products are the far end of global supply chains reaching back into rainforests — palm oil hidden in snacks, soap and cosmetics; soy feeding livestock; cocoa→chocolate; rubber in tyres and gloves; timber→furniture; and medicines from forest plants. The core skill is tracing a chain BOTH directions (forest→plantation→processing→shipping→factory→shelf→home, and the reverse), surfacing palm oil's hidden ubiquity (in roughly half of packaged supermarket products per WWF), and understanding the demand feedback loop: because demand pulls the chain, consumer choices can push back. The nuanced message is 'choose certified/sustainable', not 'boycott everything', because blanket boycotts can harm smallholder farmers and remove incentives to farm sustainably.
misconceptions: 'Rainforest products are just exotic foods' — many are hidden ingredients (palm oil in soap, rubber in tyres).
'My shopping can't affect a faraway forest' — consumer demand directly pulls the supply chain.
'Boycotting everything is best' — it can devastate smallholder livelihoods; choosing certified is usually better.
'A product with a green label is automatically fine' — certification helps but varies; it's a signal, not a guarantee.
'Soy is mainly eaten by people as tofu' — most soy feeds livestock worldwide.

activities.title: Build the chain from shelf to forest (and back)
steps: Start from a familiar supermarket product (e.g. a jar of chocolate spread) and build the chain link by link backwards: factory → ship → refinery → plantation → the land, until the last link reaches where the crop was grown, which may be recently cleared forest, at-risk forest or long-established farmland, depending on the source.
Then trace the SAME chain forwards from forest to home, saying each stage aloud or writing it, so the product is seen as the END of a chain, not an isolated thing.

Use a 'scan the basket' reveal: check other everyday items (biscuits, soap, shampoo) and discover how many contain palm oil or palm-derived ingredients. WWF estimates that roughly half of packaged supermarket products do, though the share in any one basket will vary.

For each product, toggle its sourcing from 'cheap/unsustainable' to 'certified' and watch, in this simplified illustrative model, a forest-impact meter fall while a smallholder-income meter holds. Then test boycotting EVERYTHING and see the model's farmer-income meter collapse too. Remember that the model shows a simplified idea, not measured real-world results.
activities.insight: Everyday shopping is the far end of a chain that reaches into the forest; demand pulls the chain, so the smarter lever is choosing the sustainable link and sending that signal back up the line — not buying nothing.

activities.title: Hidden ingredients hunt
steps: Read real ingredient labels on everyday packaging together (biscuits, bread, soap, shampoo), and check product descriptions or material labels for items like trainers, which do not carry ingredient lists.

List the non-obvious rainforest-linked ingredients — palm oil or palm derivatives in some soaps and breads, natural rubber in some trainer soles (many use synthetic rubber), and soy animal feed behind much meat and many eggs (not shown on the label).
Sort products into 'obvious tropical treat' (chocolate, bananas, coffee) versus 'hidden ingredient' and discuss why the hidden ones are easy to miss.
Spot certification labels where they appear (Rainforest Alliance frog, FSC, RSPO) and discuss what signal they send.
activities.insight: Rainforest products are not only exotic jungle foods — many are hidden ingredients in ordinary goods, including palm oil, soy animal feed, rubber and timber.

activities.title: Sequence and match the journey (check and consolidate)
steps: Order the stages of the palm-oil journey in sequence: forest → plantation → processing/refinery → shipping → factory → shelf → home.
Match everyday products to their hidden rainforest ingredient (biscuit→palm oil, tyre→rubber, chicken nugget→soy feed, furniture→timber).
Answer: how does choosing a certified product help a forest compared with buying carelessly OR boycotting everything?
activities.insight: Consolidates the chain order, the product→ingredient links, and the reasoning that certified sourcing is usually better than both careless buying and a blanket boycott.

activities.title: Argue the diagnostic both ways
steps: Respond to a friend's claim: 'My shopping in Britain can't possibly affect a rainforest thousands of miles away — and anyway, the best thing to do is boycott every single rainforest product.'
State clearly whether the friend is right on EACH of the two points, and explain WHY for each half.
Apply the reasoning to a NEW product of the pupil's choice: pick something used this morning and trace an ingredient back toward a rainforest, saying where to look on the label.
Discuss trade-offs: if everyone boycotted palm oil tomorrow, who is helped and who harmed; and is it fair to expect a family on a tight budget to pay more for certified goods?
activities.insight: Genuine supply-chain reasoning holds both halves: everyday shopping IS connected through demand, AND a blanket boycott is not the best answer because it harms smallholders and removes the reward for farming sustainably.

checkQuestion: A friend says: 'My shopping at the supermarket in Britain can't possibly affect a rainforest thousands of miles away — and anyway, the best thing anyone can do is boycott every single rainforest product.' Are they right on either point? Tell me WHY.
checkAnswer: Wrong on both. Ordinary shopping IS linked to rainforests: palm oil is in roughly half of packaged supermarket goods, and soy (mostly for animal feed), cocoa, coffee, natural rubber, beef and timber all come partly from cleared or at-risk forest land — consumer demand pulls the whole supply chain. But boycotting everything is not the best answer either: it can wreck the livelihoods of smallholder farmers and give them no reason to farm sustainably. The stronger choice is to buy certified sustainable products (RSPO palm oil, Rainforest Alliance, FSC), waste less, and push companies to clean up their supply chains.
